newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-New Olivetti boss raises hopes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-New Olivetti boss raises hopes.

text.p: The new man in charge of Italy's Olivetti raised hopes on Thursday the crisis-hit group may now get down to sorting out loss-making businesses but analysts cautioned many question marks still hang over its future.

The struggling information technology group has undergone a series of upheavals in the last two weeks culminating in the ousting late on Wednesday of chief executive Francesco Caio and the appointment of Roberto Colaninno in his stead.

"At last the phase of anarchy has ended. We're through the convulsions of the last two weeks. I don't think this has ended the story but probably the most difficult phase is at an end," said a Milan equity analyst who declined to be named.

"If the management talks to investors, major clients and partners and lays out a coherent strategy, then there shouldn't be further problems," said Michael Pacitti, Italian equity analyst at Jame Capel in London.
"But one of the first things they have to do is stop all the speculation (on their finances and strategy)," Pacitti said.

Relief was evident on the bourse that Olivetti's most recent turmoil was over, at least for the present, although traders warned high bids on the stock price on Thursday reflected short term speculation rather than a vote of confidence in Colaninno.

Brokers and analysts were cautious in their initial response to Colaninno's appointment and Caio's resignation, which came only two weeks after Caio won what was viewed as a boardroom battle resulting in De Benedetti's resignation as chairman.
"Once the dust has settled we can discuss where the company is heading," the Milan analyst said.
Olivetti, which has not broken even since 1990, is mired in two probes into its results for the first half of 1996, when it made a loss of 440.2 billion lire ($289 million).

Bourse watchdog Consob on Monday demanded the group answer 16 questions on its strategy, financial situation and valuation of its stocks, which the group answered by sidestepping issues most concerning the market, like the current level of its debt.

In addition, Caio, who held his post for just three months, De Benedetti and new chairman Antonio Tesone, are under preliminary investigation by magistrates at the group's home town of Ivrea. The magistrates suspect the company may have issued misleading statements about its financial position.

Brokers pointed out these problems had not vanished with the appointment of Colaninno, a close ally of De Benedetti who heads Sogefi, an auto components company controlled by De Benedetti's industrial holding CIR.
"The situation still isn't clear and the new man is considered a De Benedetti clone," said a broker in Milan.
"We have no new information to suggest it's a turnaround situation just yet and the way the stock has been moving recently, it's more like going to a casino," he added.
"As long as we're still unaware of what the group intends to do and we're ignorant of its current financial state, it would be irresponsible to be positive on the stock," another said.

Despite their caution Olivetti shares closed 11.29 percent up on the day at 567.6 lire on volume of 71 million shares. The stock had plummeted to a record low of 465 lire on Tuesday as market anxiety about the state of the group's finances reached panic levels.
Brokers said Thursday's buying interest was purely speculative. "There are some bargain hunters around. But people must buy only on risk taking accounts -- it's not for widows and orphans," one said.
